pages.title: How can one name identify one structure?

blocks.text: A label such as “alcohol” does not identify a particular bottle: methanol and ethanol are different compounds. A systematic name should let another chemist reconstruct the same arrangement of atoms. We first recognise the carbon skeleton and then identify the chemically important groups.

IUPAC nomenclature is a rule-based naming system. The parent name describes the selected main skeleton, locants are numbers locating features, prefixes name substituents, and a suffix identifies the principal functional group. Each part contributes structural information.

pages.transition: First identify whether the skeleton is a chain, a ring or a heterocycle.

pages.title: Chains, rings and different ring atoms

blocks.text: Acyclic compounds have open chains, straight or branched. Cyclic compounds contain rings. An alicyclic compound such as cyclohexane has a non-aromatic carbon ring; benzene is aromatic. If an atom other than carbon belongs to the ring, the compound is heterocyclic.

Cyclohexane and benzene both have six-carbon rings but different bonding and chemical behaviour. A ring containing oxygen is not a hydrocarbon because hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. A ring-shaped drawing alone is therefore insufficient for classification.
A locant is simply a position number. A substituent replaces a hydrogen on the chosen parent; an alkyl substituent is obtained formally by removing one hydrogen from an alkane.

pages.transition: Within that skeleton, particular atom groups determine characteristic chemistry.

pages.title: The group that changes the chemistry

blocks.text: A functional group is an atom or group that gives an organic compound characteristic chemical behaviour. –OH identifies an alcohol when attached to a saturated carbon, –CHO an aldehyde, >C=O a ketone, and –COOH a carboxylic acid.

Members of a homologous series share a functional group and general pattern of chemical behaviour; successive members differ by CH2, a mass difference of about 14 u. Methanol and ethanol belong to the alcohol series even though their physical properties are not identical.

pages.transition: With the group recognised, we can select a parent chain for its name.

pages.title: Choose the parent before numbering

blocks.text: For an alkane, select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent. The chain may bend on the page; a visually straight line is not automatically longest. Meth-, eth-, prop-, but- and pent- indicate one to five carbons; the ending –ane indicates saturated bonding.

For CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3, the longest continuous chain contains four carbons: butane. The remaining CH3 is a methyl substituent. Numbering from the nearer end puts it at carbon 2 rather than 3, so the name is 2-methylbutane.

pages.transition: The same parent must now be numbered consistently.

pages.title: Use the first point of difference

blocks.text: Compare possible locant sequences from the two ends of a parent chain. Choose the sequence with the lower number at the first point where they differ. Repeated identical substituents use di-, tri- or tetra-; their positions are all written.

CH3CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2,3-dimethylpentane. Numbering from the other end would give 3,4, so 2,3 is preferred. In a name, commas separate numbers and hyphens separate numbers from words. “Di” counts methyl groups; it does not add two carbons to the parent chain.

pages.transition: Different branch names add one more ordering decision.

pages.title: Naming more than one kind of branch

blocks.text: Different substituent names are written alphabetically. Numerical multipliers such as di- and tri- do not control that alphabetical order. If equally good numbering gives the same locant set to different substituents, alphabetical order helps decide which substituent receives the lower locant.

In 3-ethyl-4-methylhexane, ethyl is listed before methyl because e comes before m. The parent remains hexane: branches are not folded into the name as though they extended the selected chain. Check the actual structure before accepting any longest-chain choice.

pages.transition: A functional group can take priority over branches when numbering the parent.

pages.title: Let the principal group guide the name

blocks.text: When a suffix functional group is present, choose a suitable parent chain containing it and number to give that principal group the lowest possible locant. In simple cases its naming priority comes before an alkyl branch or a multiple bond.

CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 contains four carbons and an alcohol group. From the nearer end –OH is on carbon 2, so the name is butan-2-ol. CH3CH2CHO has a terminal aldehyde carbon included in its three-carbon parent and is propanal; that carbon is carbon 1.

pages.transition: We can extend that idea to unsaturation and more than one functional group.

pages.title: Multiple bonds and several groups

blocks.text: The endings –ene and –yne locate double and triple bonds. For more than one suffix group, retain the required parent ending and use multipliers: HOCH2CH2OH is ethane-1,2-diol. For more than one kind of functional group, select the principal one for the suffix and describe subordinate groups as prefixes.

CH3COCH2CH2OH has a ketone and an alcohol group. The ketone has suffix priority here; numbering gives its carbonyl carbon locant 2. The –OH group is hydroxy at carbon 4, so the compound is 4-hydroxybutan-2-one. Priority prevents calling the same compound simply a substituted alcohol.

pages.transition: Ring names use the same need for clear, minimal position numbers.

pages.title: Rings use the same need for clear positions

blocks.text: A saturated carbon ring uses cyclo- before the alkane name. A single methyl group on cyclohexane gives methylcyclohexane without an unnecessary locant 1. With two substituents, number the ring to give the lowest locants consistent with the naming rules.

A substituent is a branch attached to the chosen parent, while a functional group describes a chemical feature. The same atom count does not guarantee the same parent or suffix. Always check connectivity, principal group and numbering rather than assembling a name from familiar words.

Try reconstructing 3-ethyl-2-methylhexane. Draw the six-carbon parent, attach methyl at 2 and ethyl at 3, then supply hydrogens to valence four. Count nine carbons overall. Reconstructing a name is a useful independent check on the parent-versus-branch distinction.

pages.transition: Let us combine these decisions into a reliable naming method.

pages.title: A naming checklist with a chemical purpose

blocks.text: Classify the skeleton, identify functional groups, choose the principal group and parent, number appropriately, locate branches and unsaturation, and assemble the name. A good name preserves enough information to draw the intended structure.

An alcohol is not named only by carbon count; location matters. Branches do not alter the parent’s stated carbon count. Homologous members differ by CH2 but retain their characteristic group, while cyclic and heterocyclic categories describe the skeleton.

questions.question: Name CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH3 and explain the numbering.
questions.answer: 2-Methylbutane: the parent has four carbons and numbering from the nearer end gives 2 rather than 3.

questions.question: Why is HOCH2CH2OH ethane-1,2-diol?
questions.answer: The parent has two carbons and two alcohol groups, at carbons 1 and 2; diol identifies both groups.

questions.question: Which distinction separates a cyclic hydrocarbon from a heterocycle?
questions.answer: A cyclic hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen, while a heterocycle has a non-carbon atom in the ring.

questions.question: Name CH3CH=CHCH3.
questions.answer: But-2-ene. The longest chain has four carbons and the double bond starts at carbon 2.

questions.question: Why is CH3COCH2CH2OH named with –one rather than –ol?
questions.answer: The ketone has suffix priority over alcohol in this example, so the alcohol is represented by the prefix hydroxy.
